#1379. Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

Peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

ONE-TOUCH BRILLIANCE! ✨ Anderson, Rogers and Kane combine beautifully to double England's lead 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Cap No. 125, goal No. 90 for the skipper 👏 https://t.co/otMcxlXyps

Following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

Hall ➡️ Kane! The Newcastle fullback swings in the corner and it's the England captain who rises highest to head home 💥 https://t.co/5EhAcNZUqm

Afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

At the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he said. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”

One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

England lead! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿⚽️ A great ball from Kane and a great finish from Coufal - unfortunately for the defender, it's in the wrong net...🫣 https://t.co/h54xQnunZM

The second goal, on 40 minutes, was one for the ages. Anderson’s ball out to the right was met first time by Rogers for the cross and Kane ran into the space, as he has done so many times, to deliver a finish struck with customary assuredness. Bellingham almost flicked in Rogers’s cross on 56 minutes and from the corner that came after, Kane nodded in a header at the back post from Lewis Hall’s cross. All said, the defending was woeful but there was nothing wrong with the finish.

Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and said he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

“It means a lot,” Tuchel said. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”

Asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel said: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

But on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

“We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”

We played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

[Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find new words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

[Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone showed he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

He’s the best England player evert to wear the shirt and it’s an honour to play with him. And he’s only getting better.

A perfect night for me personally and also for the team. It’s been a tough camp, a long camp with some difficult games so it’s nice to finish it off all together. An extremely proud evening for me.

You saw some fantastic football out there tonight. The way we’re moving, the one-touch stuff, a fantastic ball from Elliot to Morgan and then a first time cross which was as good as it gets. As a striker you’re just waiting for those opportunities.

It started in the first game [reaching a higher level] although the result didn’t go for us. First game after a tournament, obviously this was a four-game camp, we had to find it [a higher level] and find it quickly. That’s the most pleasing thing.

This is the England team. There’s always going to be competition for places. It’s about taking the opportunity whether it’s 90 minutes, five minutes, whatever it was, make the most of it. You’re seeing that, everyone wants to be part of this. That’s only going to make us better for sure.

[Now for cap 126 next month?] That would be nice for sure.

That was Harry Kane’s warm-up prior to England’s 7-0 demolition of Croatia and it underlined just why the striker will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record on Tuesday night.

As demonstrated in Rijeka, Kane’s career has been a non-stop pursuit of excellence that has led him to the very top of the national game. England’s record goalscorer will also become the joint most-capped player with Shilton, when he makes his 125th appearance against the Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Eberechi Eze is set to start for England in the clash against Czech Republic tonight. The Arsenal forward is poised to come in for Anthony Gordon, who has started in the three matches during the Nations League international break. Trent Alexander-Arnold is also due to play at right-back, with Jarell Quansah moving to centre-back to cover for Ezri Konsa.

Alex Scott has been ruled out through injury, which has upset Bournemouth after he played in the win over Croatia at the weekend. Myles Lewis-Skelly is expected to get a recall to the team after playing against Czech Republic in Prague last week when England won 2-0. Morgan Rogers, who scored against Croatia, is in line to start in place of Bukayo Saka.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of England vs Czech Republic from Wembley in the fourth and mercifully final round of fixtures in this sprawling Nations League international break. Tonight Harry Kane will win his 125th cap and equal Peter Shilton for England appearances.

Shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

England played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

In the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Even their thrilling, second-half showing against Croatia in their World Cup opener in June preceded the dreary 0-0 draw with Ghana.

Given the attacking fluency in Rijeka, Thomas Tuchel must be tempted not to to ring the changes and replace seven or eight players. He will have to find replacements for the injured Alex Scott and Ezri Konsa, however, and Calvert Lewin, who has had seven minutes of action, Rio Ngumoha 19, Morgan Gibbs-White 27 and Jarrad Branthwaite one, may feel they deserve a fairer opportunity to show what they can do in a match.

#1378. O'Neill is running out of road...and the heat around him could rise extremely quickly

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 15:04 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 18:18 EDT, 2 November 2026

Moments after the tin lid was placed on a truly hideous week for Celtic with a home league defeat to Rangers, Martin O’Neill uttered some words which he later came to regret.

‘I genuinely will reflect and see,’ said the Northern Irishman when asked if he would consider his future. ‘It’s a matter of whether I can help the team. The manager is supposed to be able to do that. I will look at that this week.

‘I think every single time something crops up and things don’t go so well, age plays a part. And do you know what? They might be right. I’ll be 110 in two years’ time so it might be time to wrap it up.’

That was on September 20. Despite going into the international break on the back of two losses to Rangers and a reverse at home to Ferencvaros, with a capitulation away to LASK still in the background, O’Neill, as we know, came back for more.

The trouble is that the impasse changed very little. In the seven matches since, Celtic have won three and lost three.

The running total of clean sheets now stands at one in ten. If anyone feels that dismal sequence will improve when Besiktas come to town on Thursday, you can name your price.

With the next international break coming after Kilmarnock’s visit to Parkhead on Sunday, it feels like further self-reflection is imminent and more difficult conversations are about to take place behind the scenes.

If O’Neill and the club’s directors can identify a reason to feel that an upturn in fortunes is on the horizon, they will be in the minority.

Martin O'Neill can barely look as his Celtic side lost 2-0 to Falkirk on Sunday

In terms of results and performances, this is a team which is flatlining. It takes a leap of faith to believe that a radical improvement lies just around the corner.

For many Celtic supporters, reconciling themselves with the truth of the current situation is not easy.

In his first spell in charge at the turn of the century, O’Neill transformed their club from a laughing stock into Scotland’s dominant team and a European force to be reckoned with once again.

Last season, against all the odds, the veteran twice rode to the rescue to land an unlikely league and cup double.

Those who wished that the credits would then roll on the story of the legend’s great return have spent much of this campaign watching through the cracks in their fingers.

While O’Neill has unquestionably been the latest manager to suffer through the ineptitude of those who are supposedly running the show, nor can he be granted a free pass for what his side are routinely serving up.

The triumphs of the early 2000s and last season offer little shelter from the current storm.

Taken purely in isolation, Sunday’s loss to Falkirk could have been shrugged off as one of those unfortunate days by those stood in the visitors’ section.

The Celtic manager must wish he had quit after trophy triumph at end of last season

Celtic did have more possession than the Bairns (70.2 per cent). They had more touches inside the opposition box (44 v 15). They had more corners (14 v 0). They had more shots at goal (24 v 6). Scott Bain, the former Celtic keeper, did have a fine game.

The trouble is that the affair was no anomaly. O’Neill’s side are making a habit of showing up well in the metrics which don’t win you points and showing up badly in the only statistic which matters.

Attempting to accentuate the positives in the aftermath, the manager pointed out that the side was still better off than at this stage last year.

While this is statistically true in the Premiership — 28 points now as opposed to 26 in 2025 — that’s no cause for celebration.

Celtic were also still in the League Cup 12 months back. And after three games in the Europa League, the team had four points compared to zero being on the board at the same juncture this time. The dogs in the street know this is a team which is regressing.

O’Neill’s plea for patience in the case of new players requiring time to adapt to their new environment doesn’t cut any ice.

O'Neill's legend at the club will never diminish but this term has been his most troubling

A club which welcomed 17 new faces in the summer, six of Falkirk’s outfield players on Sunday weren’t there last season — as opposed to three of the visitors. John McGlynn doesn’t seem to have the same issues getting lesser-paid individuals assimilated to his way of working.

There have been a couple of recurring themes to Celtic under O’Neill this season. With the ball, the players lack zip, imagination and penetration. Without it, they look meek and vulnerable.

Just as Dundee United did on Wednesday, McGlynn’s side repeatedly cut them open at the weekend.

The more glaring the shortcomings become, the more legitimate it is to question if the structure of the side and the tactical approach is all that it might be.

In the days when O’Neill was able to field a team containing the likes of Paul Lambert, Lubo Moravcik and Henrik Larsson, the manager didn’t have to fret about the minor details.

With his sheer presence giving a squad brimming with top-level players added psychological strength, Celtic invariably overpowered their opponents.

Cameron Carter-Vickers and Callum McGregor have both had their say on team's tactics

Evidently, that embarrassment of riches no longer exists. Is O’Neill, at 74 years of age, capable of relaying the required tactical information to a much more limited group?

Is the correct detail forthcoming from his cadre of young coaches — Shaun Maloney, Mark Fotheringham and Stephen McManus? It’s certainly a moot point.

You could be forgiven for believing that the current crop of players have reservations about their level of tactical preparedness and the structure of the side.

Also speaking after that 1-0 loss to Rangers, Cameron Carter-Vickers claimed the team ‘played a bit too random.’

For one senior player to bemoan a lack of a plan was one thing. For another to question it set the alarm bells off.

Following the 2-2 draw with United, a match which initially saw O’Neill play two centre-forwards in Camilo Duran and Callum Osmand as wingers, skipper Callum McGregor opined that ‘the players behave like a winger, or they behave like a striker.’

He added: ‘You can get away with it for a few games, but if it’s a striker playing as a winger, you are going to get that behaviour a lot of the time.’

Over the weekend, James McClean, who played under O’Neill for Ireland, reprised the theme as he promoted his new book.

Celtic ran into an inspired Falkirk team, and a superb keeper in Scott Bain on Sunday

Recalling the bemusement of the raft of English Championship players who O’Neill called up, McClean offered: ‘Martin wasn’t big on tactics.’

Whatever accusations could justifiably be levelled at the manager and his coaching staff, those who hold them solely responsible for the current malaise are small in number.

Having got away with it — as Celtic did last season — a forward-thinking football club wouldn’t have gone back to the well by asking a septuagenarian to go again.

Not only did the Parkhead hierarchy predictably show a lack of vision by failing to appoint a younger manager with fresh ideas, they, again, failed O’Neill in the transfer market.

The selling of Arne Engels to West Ham on the eve of the season-defining clash with LASK was the latest dereliction of duty.

The six players signed in the final hours of the window — five of them loans — was the equivalent of a dash down the bargain aisle at closing time on Christmas Eve.

The board are still main target of fans, but O'Neill can't escape all the blame for poor displays on pitch

O’Neill, notably, hasn’t gone public with his dismay at the hand he was dealt in the manner in which his predecessor, Brendan Rodgers, did. But if he’s happy to toe the party line, the responsibility for a failing football team falls squarely on his shoulders.

The heat around him could rise extremely quickly. Two years after making a commendable impact in the Champions League under Rodgers, by the end of this week, an emaciated squad could find itself propping up the 36-team Europa League table.

Whether that transpires or not, the level of acrimony which constantly surrounds the club these days seems set to increase.

For O’Neill, with each passing week, a return to the comfort of a radio studio must hold greater appeal.

Four years ago, scientists reported findings from the OneK1K project1. #1374. Barry Sees Blues Beat Newcastle Again

Thierno Barry's eighth goal of the season proved enough for Everton to beat Newcastle for the second time in the space of four days in a 1-0 win at St James' Park.

Having triumphed 3-1 in the Carabao Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Blues left the North East with three Premier League points this time around.

Following a dominant first-half display, Everton got their reward four minutes after the restart when keeper Lukas Hornicek spilled Tyrique George's low shot, allowing Barry to tap home from a yard out.

That proved decisive to continue the Toffees' fine recent record at St James' Park – with a third victory on the trot – as David Moyes' men moved up to seventh in the Premier League table.

Moyes made two changes from the team that beat the Magpies 3-1 in the Carabao Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium four days earlier – Jarrad Branthwaite returning from a concussion protocol and Harrison Armstrong preferred to Hayden Hackney in central midfield.

Branthwaite partnering James Tarkowski in central defence saw Jake O'Brien switch to right-back, with Merlin Röhl getting the nod ahead of Tyler Dibling to play in front of the Irishman.

Buoyed by their success over Matthias Jaissle's team on Merseyside last week, the Blues made an excellent start and did not look back in a dominant first half that had everything but a deserved opener.

Röhl was the first to threaten when he collected a pass from Thierno Barry and drove a rising first-time angled shot narrowly over the bar, before Barry failed to get a clean connection from seven yards out after Jarrad Branthwaite headed down Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's free-kick into the striker's path.

Everton then had two more opportunities to edge ahead in two minutes of first-half added-time. Dewsbury-Hall's glorious curling cross from the left edge of the area narrowly evaded O'Brien lurking at the back post. And the Toffees' No.8 turned provider again seconds later, getting the freedom down the left flank to cut back to Armstrong, who screwed his first-time finish wide when well placed from 12 yards out.

Thankfully, the Toffees did not have to wait long to find the back of the net after the restart. Four minutes into the second half, James Garner slid George in through the left channel and, when the winger's shot squeezed through the hands of Hornicek, Barry was left with the simple task of tucking home from a yard out.

With the wind in their sails, Everton went close to a second as Branthwaite's header was turned over the bar by Hornicek, before the Newcastle keeper did the same with Dewsbury-Hall's whipped shot from 25 yards out.

And from the resulting corner, Garner picked out O'Brien at the back post to nod down a goalbound header which Hornicek did well to turn behind.

Having done little to worry Jordan Pickford up until the hour mark, the hosts went so close to levelling when substitute Yoane Wissa nodded into Anthony Elanga at the back post who squeezed a finish under the England No.1 but, thankfully, the ball rolled along the line before being booted clear by Tarkowski.

As the inevitable Newcastle pressure grew trying to find a leveller, substitute Jacob Ramsey hit a volley from the edge of the area with 11 minutes remaining that crept inches past the left-hand post.

Then, as eight minutes of injury-time approached, Wissa looked to apply a finish from close range only to be denied by the legs of Pickford.

And that was to prove crucial as Everton saw out the closing stages, Ramsey being given his marching orders with seconds remaining after picking up two quick yellow cards for late tackles on substitute Hackney and then Armstrong.

Long international break, we recovered most of our players and have a point to prove after our last game.

[Declan Rice] needed that [break] after everything he’s done over the years. He has looked fresh this week.

There’s no doubt who the biggest threat to Arsenal’s defence will be today: Dominic Calvert-Lewin has four goals in six games in all competitions this season and is the top scoring Englishman in the league since the start of last season. Right, where were we? Three weeks on from the fifth round of Premier League fixtures in which the champions Arsenal were beaten 3-0 by Brighton and todays’ visitors, Leeds United, who remain unbeaten, drew in a tepid goalless fixture with Crystal Palace, we finally get to the sixth. As worrying as the result was at the Amex, Arsenal still created a shedload of chances and last season they were the one club that battered Leeds in both games – first early in the season when they were playing four at the back and before Dominic Calvert-Lewin, a late signing, was fully fit, and then later after they had successfully switched to a “base formation” of three centre-backs and the tactical flexibility that allowed.

It was a 5-0 tanking in August and 4-0 in January, so to say Leeds travel to a ground at which they have never won more in hope than expectation would be as true as much as it is hackneyed. Adding to a sense of foreboding and thanks to Opta’s excellent Jonny Cooper, we also have to take into account the fact that Leeds, floodlight kings, have not won a Premier League match kicking off before 3pm since August 2022 and have not won a match in London since beating Brentford in May that year to save themselves from relegation. However, they do boast the division’s best defensive record – three goals conceded – and the No1 ranked goalkeeper in James Trafford who has a save percentage of 87. For all the sense of doom, though, Leeds have become a very good side and their spine – Trafford–Muharemovic–Ampadu–Calvert-Lewin marries steel and class.

Arsenall need no fanfare. Until the set-back in dear old Sussex by the sea, they had looked formidable most of the time and will have been champing at the bit to get back out there and prove it was an aberration. Mikel Arteta mentioned he has doubts about Declan Rice, Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa but Ben White, Max Dowman and Chrsthian Mosquera are all available. For Leeds Joe Rodon is still out and Dan James was injured on international duty but Harry Wilson and Jean-Matteo Bahoya returned to training after knocks this week and Daniel Farke was relatively optimistic about their prospects.

#1370. Michael Carrick's next nightmare: How Aston Villa misfit Donyell Malen became Europe's hottest striker... as Roma star looks to pile on the misery for Man United in Champions League

Published: 02:00 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 04:31 EDT, 3 November 2026

It’s been a brutal start to the season for Manchester United, who are winless in nine games on the spin.

And as Michael Carrick fights to save his job, they must now find a way to deal with the most potent forward in Europe’s top five leagues.

Donyell Malen, the reinvented centre-forward, has caught fire in Italy, a world away from the talented but unspectacular winger who left Aston Villa.

The 27-year-old arrives at Old Trafford on Tuesday as Europe’s most prolific striker, with Roma unbeaten in Serie A. Villa let him go for just £25million.

Roma are contenders in Serie A, and Malen’s goals are the biggest reason why.

The Dutchman has totalled 22 goals in 2026. That is more than any player in the big five leagues, including newly crowned Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane.

At Villa, it never quite happened for him. Malen arrived from Borussia Dortmund in January 2025 - the same window as Jhon Duran’s departure - but he spent most of his minutes out wide and never nailed down a starting place. Neither wing suited a player miscast as a pacey wideman.

Donyell Malen has scored 22 league goals in 2026 - more than even Harry Kane

Malen played just one and a half seasons at Villa Park, scoring 10 goals in 46 games

The Dutchman scored just 10 goals in 46 games at Villa Park, which hid his quality. He grew into his second season and was named Villa’s Player of the Month in November; but two months later, he was sold.

'It was my decision,' Malen told Italian media. 'I wanted to play and be part of a team where I could take the field every weekend and play an important role. At that stage, I didn’t feel important, so I think I made the best choice.

'Today I feel I’m in the right place with the right people. The coach and my teammates show a lot of confidence in me, and together, all of this is helping me become the player I dreamed of being.'

The signs of improvement were here before this summer's World Cup, though Malen  could not find the net despite starting all three Netherlands group games. Brian Brobbey was the side's focal point, returning Malen to a supporting role alongside Cody Gakpo.

It was a surprise to Dutch fans, who remember the centre forward terrorising defences at PSV, where he scored 19 goals and added eight assists in his final full season in 2020-21.

Roma boss Gian Piero Gasperini, who joined the club the previous summer, had moved Malen into a role he had not played in years: striker. The result was an outrageous 14 goals in 18 games to finish the season.

Malen has struck up a potent partnership with Paulo Dybala

Malen has rewarded his manager’s faith by helping secure Champions League football, a level the club have not reached since 2018.

Position is only part of the story. Once forced to create chances, Malen now finishes them. Argentine wizards Matias Soule and Paulo Dybala are his accomplices in a stellar front three, feeding him the best service in Europe.

Starting alongside Dybala, Malen got off to the perfect start to the season with a hat-trick in a 4-0 home win over Fiorentina.

'Getting off to such a good start by scoring a hat-trick was crucial,' he said. 'As a team we were strong and connected, and I immediately had a very good feeling. We can build on moments like these and do something special. Paulo and I clicked immediately.'

When Dybala’s constant niggles strike, new signing Rodrigo Mora has proved more than an adequate stand-in, helping to spearhead Roma’s title charge.

Gasperini has built a career on finding diamonds in the dirt. Alejandro ‘Papu’ Gómez, Josip Ilicic and Ademola Lookman all owe him a debt of gratitude.

Malen is not the only one from the Premier League’s discard pile to find new life in Serie A. Romelu Lukaku, Gianluca Scamacca, Scott McTominay and Rasmus Hojlund have all thrived there.

Even Tottenham flop Kolo Muani enjoyed an excellent six months in his first spell in Italy.

United's beleagured defence must find a way to stop Malen and avoid more humiliation

It hasn’t always worked - Evan Ferguson and Leon Bailey both disappointed at Roma - but it certainly has for Malen. Villa, meanwhile, can only watch. The sale allowed them to break roughly even, but it left supporters frustrated, with Duran, Moussa Diaby and Jacob Ramsey also sold in recent years.

It came as the club worked within the Premier League’s financial constraints.

Now Roma throw down the gauntlet at Old Trafford, and it could turn from bad to ugly for United.

'I don't think so much about the idol I'm becoming for the fans, I just want to score a lot of goals,' Malen said a few weeks ago. 'We have team goals to achieve and I'm focused on that.'

Malen’s eyes should light up against a volatile defence. A big night would push him further up the race for 2026-27’s top scorer and show English football the talent it only glimpsed.

#1369. How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

Science in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: 22% of participants in that nation said they had ‘no trust at all’ in science in 2025. Credit: Thomas Imo/Photothek via Getty

Trust in science and researchers has fallen following the COVID-19 pandemic, the largest survey of public confidence in science shows. Led by the global biomedical funder Wellcome in London and published on 10 October, it explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence (see ‘Trust in decline’).

“We should be paying attention to, and thinking about, what needs to be done to earn that trust,” says Philippa Michael, head of public initiatives at Wellcome, who led the project. This is the third survey of its kind conducted by Wellcome, following editions in 2018 and 2020.

The analysis points to a “mixed” picture that varies between countries and regions, says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia (see ‘Regional differences’).

The study also shows a connection between science and people’s broader experiences, including their perceived financial security, says Michael (see ’Money matters‘).

“If people feel economically insecure, then they’re going to feel a greater distance between themselves and science and scientists,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat, at Harvard Kennedy School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This disconnect “is not about science’s efficacy or its ability to fix problems”, he adds.

The survey found that countries where people reported high confidence in hospitals and health-care clinics were “more likely to have greater trust in science”, notes Michael. Levels of trust were also high in respondents who were confident in accessing health-care services when needed. “It’s really essential that science is credible, relevant and beneficial to people in their lives,” Michael adds.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03248-z

#1367. Emery would be mad to go to United - his best route to the top is at Villa. They're close to being giants and, with him as boss, they can bridge the gap to the elite: OLIVER HOLT

Published: 04:22 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 06:11 EDT, 3 November 2026

Unai Emery, the man of the moment, the manager whose name is on everybody’s lips, the man that others would make their king, walked into the cavernous press conference room at the Nou Camp just after 8.15pm local time on Monday evening.

This is only a league game, early in the competition but there was electricity in the room that comes with the anticipation of the collision ahead. ‘This is elite football and Barcelona is always the favourite in a competition like this,’ Emery reminded his audience, ‘but we also have a history.

‘In 1982, we won the Champions League, the so-called European Cup. Barcelona are the favourites because of the present and what they have done over the last ten years. We are constantly seeking new challenges. We want to come here tomorrow night and see how far away we are from Barcelona.’

This is Emery against a big club. Against one of the modern elite. This is Emery and his wits against Lamine Yamal and Rodri and Raphinha. This is what Jamie Carragher, one of Emery’s most vocal – and controversial - champions of recent days, would call a ‘giant’ club. The phrase ‘Mes Que Un Club’ is even written into the seats at this magnificent stadium. It is the kind of club many believe Emery is born for.

Everybody is lavishing praise upon him. A few hours earlier, at the Barcelona training complex in Sant Joan Despi, several miles west of the city, Hansi Flick, the Barca coach, waxed lyrical about Emery’s talents and said he was the reason they were expecting such a tough match in their Champions League tie here on Tuesday evening.

‘Unai Emery is one of the best coaches in Europe and the world,’ Flick said. ‘He is very successful. In the way his team plays, you can see a clear structure in defence. And in offence, they have different patterns. For me, it is amazing to see his team.

At the Barcelona training complex, Hansi Flick, the Barca coach, waxed lyrical about Emery’s talents and said he was the reason they were expecting such a tough match

Flick also praised Nicolas Jackson, the Villa striker who has found his form under Emery

‘Their start this season was not easy, but they came back. You can see the confidence they have on the ball, how they play out, and Nicolas Jackson is at an unbelievable level. For us, it will be a tough game against a good team and, as well, a great coach.’

Anthony Gordon, who joined Barcelona from Newcastle United in the summer, had already given a press conference of impressive maturity and thoughtfulness that had taken in his love of books and his distrust of TikTok but he, too, was unstinting in his admiration for Emery.

'Villa are a very good team,’ Gordon said. ‘They have one of the best coaches in the world right now. They are on a great run of late as well, so it will be a difficult game. They are one of the teams who are always in a game and are always ready for any type of game. It will be a very tough challenge.’

Even the environs of the stadium seemed to pay homage to Emery’s talents. Cranes still lean over the stands here as the extensive renovations to the steepling stands continue. Emery, we all know, is the master of the rebuild.

So by the time Emery walked out into that auditorium, it felt almost as if this were a final audition. This is the kind of stuff that, understandably, enrages Villa and their fans because of its patronising tone but the more impressive his results with his club, the more people suggest he should go elsewhere.

That is what got Carragher in trouble. Carragher said Manchester United should be making him their number one target because he is the best manager in the league. ‘Surely, he would want the opportunity to manage a giant again,’ Carragher said, aiming a couple of expletives at Villa supporters for good measure.

Villa chairman Nassef Sawiris threatened to take legal action against Carragher, Carragher apologised and all was forgotten. But while Emery thrives and a manager at one of the elite European clubs struggles, he will continue to be linked to those positions. It is the way it has always been.

And anyway, Emery would be mad to go to United if Michael Carrick leaves Old Trafford in the next few weeks. Not just because United is a basket-case of a club run by people who would not allow the manager to have anything like the level of control he enjoys at Villa, where he has smart owners who trust him and support him to the hilt.

Emery has been talked about as a successor to Michael Carrick at Manchester United

Emery knows what it can be like at so-called bigger clubs like PSG and Arsenal, when impatience runs wild and expectations are absurd and support starts to wane. His best route to the very top is at a club like Villa. Because Villa are close to being giants and, with him as boss, they can bridge the gap to the elite.

Emery lost most of his first team in the summer - Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Lucas Digne, Emiliano Martinez, Youri Tielemans, Ollie Watkins, Donyell Malen and Leon Bailey all left – but he has fashioned a new exciting side in their stead already.

Villa are unbeaten in their last five games in the Premier League, including a victory that handed Manchester City their first defeat of the season, and sit second only to PSG at the top of the nascent Champions League table, with three straight wins. Emery is burnishing his reputation as a football magician. He is the game’s hottest managerial property again.

If Villa get a result at the Nou Camp, speculation about the future of Emery, who will turn 55 on the day of the game, will run wild again. It is bound to. It is a compliment to both manager and club, although it is unlikely Villa will see it that way. The joy of the results he is producing is tempered only by the fear of losing him.

But for all his success in Europe – he has won the Europa League five times, most recently with Villa in Istanbul last summer – he has a miserable record at the Nou Camp. He has brought six different clubs here and lost 14 of the 15 matches he has managed. His sole victory was with Villarreal in May 2022.

He has one particular ghost to slay in this competition. Because the Nou Camp was the scene of La Remontada, or ‘the comeback’, when Emery’s PSG brought a 4-0 lead to Barcelona for the second leg of a Round of 16 tie. PSG had won the first leg at the Parc des Princes 4-0 in March 2017 but Barcelona swept them aside 6-1 back in Catalonia.

The mention of that game was the one time during the press conference when Emery bristled. When asked what his memory of it was, he said sharply: ‘One more.’ Just one game among hundreds, he seemed to be saying. ‘I played in Europe 16 years in a row and I have learned in all of them. I learned so, so much. That night, I learned on sports side and not the sports side.’

Alongside him, John McGinn spoke compellingly, too. He spoke about coming here just once before, on a stadium tour when he was eight years old and he and his family were on their way to a holiday in the Canary Islands.

Emery has one particular ghost to slay in this competition because the Nou Camp was the scene of La Remontada, when his PSG side lost despite coming with a 4-0 lead in the first leg

‘I am 32 years old and the trajectory of this club is allowing me to dream the dream of playing in front of the biggest crowds in the biggest arenas,’ McGinn said. ‘We want to make this a yearly experience to compete with the biggest teams in England and Europe.’

Emery also mentioned Gordon as one of the components he admires in the Barcelona side. Listening to him earlier, it was clear that he has already grown, both on and off the pitch since his move to Spanish football.

‘The challenge of joining Barca is different to what I've had before,’ Gordon said, ‘because when I was at Everton, I was fighting relegation for two or three years, which was tough. At Newcastle we were fighting for the Champions League and to push up the tables, and now I am at a club where we are fighting for every trophy.

‘I really enjoyed all three because they come with different things to help you as a person, help you grow. I think to be competing on every front for every trophy is definitely the most enjoyable. I think people think it's more pressure, but it's actually less pressure than fighting relegation and fighting to push up the table for the Champions League. I want to win every trophy. I want to be the best. This club allows me to do so.’

Before he left, Gordon spoke about how he rations his time on social media and reads more books and goes on more walks. ‘When you're in that wheel of dopamine addiction and you're scrolling on social media, you have to come away from it and get back to what’s real,’ he said.

On Tuesday night in the Nou Camp, Emery and Villa will take the next step on their advance on Europe and the rest of us will find out what is real and what is not.

#1365. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1363. Asia Cup is POSTPONED just two months before its start due to safety concerns in Saudi Arabia - in huge boost to Premier League clubs

Published: 03:25 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 06:13 EDT, 3 November 2026

The 2027 Asia Cup has been delayed by almost a year amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

Less than two months before it was due to kick off, the tournament hosted by Saudi Arabia has been postponed until December 2027 after the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict re-escalated.

Major airports in Saudi Arabia are operating reduced services after a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people. Two people were also killed after an attack at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

It makes the tournament not only a logistical nightmare for the 24 participating teams but also raises serious safety concerns.

A statement from the Asian Football Confederation said: 'The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved rescheduling the flagship national team tournament considering the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions.

'The new dates of the tournament (December 23 2027 to January 21 2028) will be presented to FIFA for approval.

'Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the Competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.'

However, the delay boosts several Premier League clubs, who no longer face losing players for up to a month of the season. Japan had ten Premier League players available for selection, with Aston Villa potentially losing first-choice goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.

Aston Villa could have been without Zion Suzuki, who has kept three clean sheets this season, for five Premier League matches and their last two league phase matches in the Champions League

Japan international Daichi Kamada has started all nine of Crystal Palace's Premier League matches this season

Crystal Palace could have been without Takehiro Tomiyasu and Daichi Kamada for up to five Premier League matches had Japan reached the final.

Ipswich's Daizen Maeda, who has made ten appearances this season, was likely to be called up alongside Brighton's Kaoru Mitoma, who is currently sidelined.

Manchester City, meanwhile, were expected to lose Uzbek international Abdukodir Khusanov.

This is the second successive tournament to be postponed after the 2023 edition was delayed by a year due to the Covid pandemic.

The Asia Cup is not the first event in Saudi Arabia to be disrupted after the PIF-backed Asian Tour Saudi International golf tournament was indefinitely postponed.

Meanwhile, the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament - featuring Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev - in Riyadh has been cancelled.

It is not a complete whitewash, though. Last weekend, Canelo Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title, beating Christian Mbilli on points in Riyadh. Riyadh will also play host to WWE Crown Jewel on Saturday.

The Formula 1 season concludes in the Middle East, with the penultimate race taking place in Qatar at the end of the month, followed by the season finale in Abu Dhabi at the start of December.

F1 intends to go ahead with both races but is continuing to monitor the situation.

Meanwhile, the second race of next season is scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia in mid-March. There are currently no plans to cancel the event, despite this year's race having been called off.

Signed match-winning shirts from Everton's Premier League victory at Newcastle United on Monday night are now up for auction in order to raise funds for the Royal British Legion.

Evertonians are able to bid on match-worn shirts from two Men’s and Women’s fixtures this month, all individually signed and bearing the poppy in memory of the fallen and Remembrance.

In addition to the clash at St James' Park, the shirts worn by the Men's team at home to Coventry City on Friday 6 November will be up for grabs, while Everton Women’s players will wear poppies for the trip to Chelsea in the Barclays Women’s Super League on Saturday 7 November and at home to Durham Women in the Subway Players Cup on Wednesday 11 November.   The Men’s game against Coventry and Everton Women’s meeting with Durham will be the Club’s two dedicated Remembrance fixtures.   Match-worn and match-issued shirts for all the above games will be signed by the respective players and auctioned online via matchwornshirt.com.

Proceeds from the auctions will go to the Royal British Legion’s Poppy Appeal to boost their year-round support of the armed forces community, including serving personnel, veterans and their families.     The first auction, for shirts worn by the Men’s team at Newcastle United, is now OPEN and will run until 5pm on Saturday 14 November.

#1360. Jude Bellingham's Dad scores SEVEN for England's OVER-50s side on same day superstar son nets for Real Madrid

Published: 06:17 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 06:18 EDT, 3 November 2026

Jude Bellingham's father Mark scored seven goals as he represented an England veterans side in a match against the Republic of Ireland.

Bellingham played up front for England Veterans' Over 50s side in a 13-1 victory on Sunday.

The 50-year-old struck six times in the first half of the match and provided an assist to give England a 7-0 lead at the break.

Bellingham added his seventh of the match in the second half as the England side cruised to victory.

Mark's goalscoring feat came on the same day that superstar son Jude scored in Real Madrid's 3-0 victory over Racing de Santander in LaLiga.

The Bellingham family were denied a unique hat-trick over the weekend, with Jobe having seen a goal ruled out as Borussia Dortmund were beaten 2-1 by Bayern Munich on Saturday.

Mark Bellingham, circled, scored seven goals for England Veterans' Over 50's team against the Republic of Ireland on Sunday. Source: Facebook/EVFC

The father of Real Madrid superstar Jude, 23, and Borussia Dortmund midfielder Jobe, Mark played for the England Veterans' Over 50's side for the first time (Source: judebellingham/Instagram)

The Bellingham family came close to a unique hat-trick at the weekend as Jude scored for Real Madrid, but Jobe had a goal disallowed as Borussia Dortmund lost to Bayern Munich

A talented non-league striker in his heyday, Mark Bellingham netted over 700 goals across at least 20 different clubs, including Leamington, Stourbridge and Sutton Coldfield Town.

He even earned the nickname the 'Non-League Pele' during his 25-year career, which ended in 2017.

Mark made his first appearance for England Veterans Over 50s side, who were crowned Seniors World Cup champions this year, clinching their ninth title in Thailand.

When not playing football of his own, Bellingham is regularly seen attending his two sons' matches.

A Southend United supporter, Mark introduced Jude to football, with the England star's first live matches coming alongside his father at Roots Hall.

Speaking about his father in a recent interview, Jude said: 'We talk about footballing heroes, and my dad was like my first.

'When you go and watch him play every week in non-league, you know it's not the Premier League or anything, but seeing the way that he played and the atmosphere, it made me fall in love with football so he was probably my first hero.

'After the first few times of going, I'd start to pay a bit more attention to the games and stuff, the atmosphere and he's scoring goals so you see him celebrating and stuff like that - you want that to be me.

'Growing up, he'd always give me tips on what I could do and now it gets to a certain age and it sort of flips and that's brilliant because we have that sort of relationship like father and son and then as I got older, like coach and player.'

Mark helped set up Stourbridge Juniors, Jude’s first club, and was a sergeant before fully focusing on his sons’ careers.

He became their agent and negotiated Jude’s £88.5million transfer to Real Madrid from Borussia Dortmund in 2023, and dealt with Dortmund again when Jobe moved there from Sunderland in 2025.

A former West Midlands Police officer, Bellingham earned the nickname the 'Non-League Pele' during his 25-year career. Pictured above with Jude (Source: CJPhillips1982/X)

Mark and Jude and Jobe's mother, Denise, are understood to have separated but remain close, the pair having attended Jude's games at the World Cup together this past summer

While in Germany, Mark reportedly held an emotional discussion with Dortmund sporting director Sebastian Kehl after being left unhappy by Jobe's substitution at half-time during his Bundesliga debut.

German publication BILD added at the time that Mark sought a meeting with manager Niko Kovac directly – and 'made no secret of his opinion'. The club proceeded to ban all family members from the dressing room following the incident.

Mark’s influence as an agent is said to have stretched to Jude’s media duties when with England. Notably, the player has gone out of his way to speak more at this most recent World Cup, but at previous tournaments he had avoided speaking beyond his obligations despite his increasing influence within the squad.

Mark and Jude and Jobe's mother, Denise, are understood to have separated but remain close, the pair having attended Jude's games at the World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico this past summer.

Dewsbury-Hall has been in outstanding form for the Toffees, picking up the Player of the Match award for Monday night’s 1-0 victory at Newcastle United – just days after another fine display in Everton’s 3-1 win over the Magpies in the Carabao Cup.

Skipper Tarkowski says his teammate has “developed a confidence to want to make the difference” – and Dewsbury-Hall epitomised that throughout a well-rounded showing last night at St James’ Park.

“No, he's top level. He really is. I think he's developed a confidence now where he wants to be the one to make the difference all the time.

#1357. West Ham star's WAG aims brutal parting dig at Nuno Espirito Santo after Hammers sacked under-fire manager - while team-mate 'likes' club post confirming his exit

Published: 03:40 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 06:25 EDT, 3 November 2026

Nuno Espirito Santo has been sacked by West Ham after a difficult start to the season, with Scott Parker poised to take over.

The Championship promotion favourites are eighth, so far struggling to live up to their billing after being relegated from the Premier League last season.

The former Tottenham, Wolves and Nottingham Forest manager, 52, signed a three-year contract in September 2025 but failed to stop the Hammers from crashing out of the top flight after a poor start to the season.

They were expected to start strongly in the second tier, yet Saturday's 3-1 home defeat by West Bromwich Albion left them with just six wins in 13 matches before Nuno's fate was confirmed on Tuesday morning.

Shortly after that news was confirmed, Marrion Areola, wife of West Ham's back-up keeper Alphonse, aimed a brutal parting dig at Nuno on her Instagram account.

Marrion, who had previously attacked Nuno after last season's relegation for dropping her husband, shared a series of Instagram stories where she appeared to express her joy at the news.

Nuno Espirito Santo has been sacked by West Ham with the club eighth in the Championship

Marrion Areola, wife of West Ham keeper Alphonse, aimed a brutal parting shot at Nuno

In one, she was smiling and posing for a photo, while in another she was skipping through the streets with Sam Phillips' 'Happy' song playing in the background.

In a third story, she shared a video from the famous film Sound of Music of So Long Farewell being sung.

Within the song, which is performed by the seven von Trapp children, a series of lyrics including 'so long', 'farewell', 'good night', 'Auf Wiedersehen', 'Adieu' and 'Au revoir' are mentioned in what is believed to her parting shot at Nuno.

West Ham's Instagram post announcing Nuno's exit, meanwhile, was liked by out of favour Mexican midfielder Edson Alvarez, who is yet to feature in the Championship this season.

George Earthy, a former academy graduate who now plays for Reading, also appeared to like the post.

Back in the summer, Marrion had taken to social media to target Nuno and former boss Graham Potter in a series of posts, blaming the pair for West Ham's relegation and hitting out at the pair for dropping her husband.

Marrion initially shared an image of Areola holding up the Conference League trophy in 2023 and stated: 'From a trophy to relegation. Thank you Potter for the start of this season and Nuno for the end.'

In another, Marrion accused Nuno of dropping her husband - who lost his place to Mads Hermansen - 'for no particular reason'.

'Being dropped at the beginning of the season for no reason,' Marrion wrote. 'Being back after a very bad start and then has made 20 games and all of a sudden: "I'm really sorry - you won't start", "Why?", "For no particular reason but I'm sorry".'

Marrion also shared a post from December that stated Areola had the highest save percentage in the Premier League, before adding on the club's relegation: 'Very sad day for the fans. Very frustrated for the family. But always proud of you no matter what.'

She then placed the blame on Nuno for Areola missing out on France's squad for the World Cup.

Sharing highlights from Areola's five appearances for France's national team she wrote: 'And NO World Cup this year, thank you Nuno'.

Meanwhile, it is understood that Parker is set to replace the Portuguese boss, with the former West Ham midfielder having been out of work since leaving Burnley shortly after their relegation from the Premier League was confirmed last season.

Parker, who has won promotion to the top flight as a manager with Fulham, Bournemouth and the Clarets, made 129 appearances for the Hammers between 2007 and 2012, winning three Player of the Year awards during his time at the club.

Former West Ham midfielder Scott Parker is poised to replace Nuno at the London Stadium

Nuno's dismissal comes after the Hammers were beaten 3-1 by West Brom on Saturday

In a club statement on Tuesday morning, West Ham had said: 'West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team Head Coach Nuno Espirito Santo has left his position with immediate effect.

'Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the Board of Directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.

'Assistant Head Coach Rui Pedro Silva and Goalkeeper Coach Rui Barbosa have also departed.

'West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.

'The process of recruiting a new Head Coach is already underway.'

The club added that Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville would take temporary charge of the team ahead of Wednesday's trip to Cardiff City.

However, it is believed that Parker will be in charge for that game if a deal is agreed in time, and that Noble, a former team-mate of his, could be part of his backroom team.

Many had expected Nuno to depart in the aftermath of relegation – and Daily Mail Sport understands that Hammers co-owner David Sullivan wanted to part ways with the Portuguese coach – but Daniel Kretinsky, now the club's largest shareholder, backed him to lead the club's promotion charge.

After that decision, the club released a statement outlining their plans and revealed that Nuno was 'highly motivated' for the challenge ahead.

Despite the high-profile sales of Mateus Fernandes and Crysencio Summerville in the summer, West Ham kept the likes of Jarrod Bowen, Tomas Soucek, Taty Castellanos and Konstantinos Mavropanos.

They also invested heavily in the squad, which included the addition of Arne Engels from Celtic for a Championship record fee of £22million.

Although they picked up 6-0 victories over Wrexham and Lincoln City, Nuno's side struggled for consistency, and back-to-back defeats by Southampton and West Brom in recent weeks proved to be the final straw.

During and after the defeat by the Baggies, home fans at the London Stadium turned on Nuno and subjected him to chants of 'sacked in the morning'.

Speaking to the media afterwards, Nuno outlined his desire to turn things around.

'Every day there is pressure,' he said. 'I’m disappointed because we wanted to improve things. We want to win matches.

'This (the chants) is the reality. You can only change this if we win games. That’s the solution: getting better results. We have to go back to good performances.

'We dropped points against Burnley (in the season opener), we lost (at home) to Charlton, Southampton and West Brom. The only solution is to improve our game. When we do that, our fans are going to stick with us. They’re going to support us.'

West Ham co-owner David Sullivan had wanted to part ways with Nuno back in the summer

West Ham have suffered back-to-back defeats after last season's Premier League relegation

There is a certain irony to the defeat by West Brom being the end for Nuno given he is a legendary former manager of their arch-rivals Wolves.

But, despite an upturn in form at the back-end of last season and an eight-game unbeaten run earlier in this campaign, he departs the London Stadium with a record of 19 wins, 19 defeats and 15 draws from 53 matches in charge.

After the Cardiff game, West Ham – who are six points adrift of table-toppers Middlesbrough – face a trip to Blackburn before the two-week international break.
